findings.title: Guided streamed response can retain serialized secret bytes and block the caller indefinitely
findings.trigger: After accepting a secret-bearing dispatch, the peer sends response headers (200 or an error status) and fewer than 1,048,577 body bytes, then leaves the body open without EOF. No independent interruption is required by this path.
findings.sourceProof: BodyHandlers.ofInputStream returns after headers. readNBytes then blocks outside the HttpRequest timeout. The status is checked only after this read. Owned requestBytes remain referenced until finally; no response-body deadline or cancellation handler closes the stream. Installed gate Java21 HttpResponse docs and MultiExchange response-header cancelTimer confirm the timeout gap.
findings.impact: Unbounded backend thread/HTTP resource use and live owned serialized secret bytes after the intended bounded call/session lifetime. This is not a claim of a persisted or externally disclosed canary.
canonicalBasis: AC-9 owned byte[] erasure after send / I-A2
AC-13 bounded recovery and honest uncertainty
findings.evidenceLevel: SOURCE_CONFIRMED; actual production HTTPS reproduction pending

findings.exactReversibleRemediation: In this existing private sender, enforce one monotonic end-to-end bound covering request plus bounded response body (at most the existing 15-second transport timeout, shortened by authentic existing caller cancellation/deadline where available). Cancel/close the stream on expiry/interruption and complete cleanup, rather than assuming HttpRequest.timeout covers stream reads. Keep the 1MiB response limit. Zero owned request bytes when request consumption is safely finished and on every bounded exit; do not erase while the publisher could still consume them. Preserve code-only UNKNOWN_OUTCOME on ambiguous dispatch, consumed admission, zero retries/extra reads/sends and existing wire/identity.
findings.owner: B after root releases concrete repair scope
findings.requiredRootCheck: Actual local HTTPS server: 200 headers+partial never-ended body and error headers+partial never-ended body; assert bounded return/stream close/owned request-byte and char-array erasure, one consumed admission/read/send, UNKNOWN_OUTCOME and recovery zero extra read/send. Add interruption/current deadline and ordinary success/failure controls. Explicitly verify production sender, not just a JDK primitive.

findings.title: Oversized Vault response bypasses explicit erasure of the owned read buffer
findings.trigger: A scoped successful Vault secret GET returns more than maxResponseBytes. The owned limit+1 byte array can contain the secret value; readBody throws before returning it to read() and its zeroing finally.
findings.sourceProof: Normal read() zeroes returned bytes around parse. readBody() throws on oversize without zeroing its locally owned bytes. The array becomes GC-eligible with unchanged content.
findings.impact: Avoidable residual in an application-owned rejected-response buffer; no live-reference leak, durable sink leak or external disclosure is demonstrated. Named HttpClient/TLS/parser residuals are not proof of erasure of this array.
findings.exactReversibleRemediation: Erase bytes in the oversize branch before throwing the existing code-only exception. Preserve the same response cap, timeout, error classification, no parse/truncation and no extra provider call.
findings.requiredRootCheck: Bounded oversized successful secret response with a planted canary in the returned prefix; capture the actual owned read-array at a test seam and assert it is zero after rejection; resolver returns no release value/version, and existing response-limit behavior remains.
